questions.prompt: Why is network isolation usually preferable to powering off a compromised host?
options: Powering off is slower to perform
Isolation achieves containment while preserving memory, which power-off destroys completely
questions.explanation: Both stop the attacker's access, but power-off eliminates the entire top of the volatility list. Isolation should be the default, with power-off a deliberate decision when active destruction outpaces it.

questions.prompt: Why should a triage collection tool not be run before memory acquisition?
options: Triage tools cannot run on live systems
The collection tool itself modifies the memory you were about to capture
Memory acquisition requires a reboot first
questions.explanation: Anything executed on the host changes memory. Capturing memory first minimizes the footprint of your own tooling on the evidence.

questions.prompt: How does retention-based volatility differ from the classic RFC 3227 model?
options: It does not; the models are identical
Logs expiring on a retention schedule are volatile on a different clock than power loss -- a log deleted next week is as perishable as RAM
Retention only applies to physical media
questions.explanation: The generalized principle is to collect first whatever will exist for the shortest time, whether the mechanism is power loss or a retention policy.

questions.prompt: Which two steps in a live response are most often skipped and cannot be repeated later?
options: Memory capture and collection of short-retention logs
questions.explanation: Both are irreversibly lost with time -- memory to power state or overwriting, short-retention logs to their expiry schedule.
